intro: Read the deck for the content and these notes for the thinking. Each note says why a slide matters, how to remember it and where practice goes wrong. Try the exercises on a real child or class you know, and write your own observations in the margin.

sections.title: What SEL Is (and Is Not)
sections.big_idea: SEL is a set of **teachable skills** that good teachers have always used, and the first step is to describe a child in terms of skills.
in_plain_words: Social and emotional learning is the process of acquiring and applying the knowledge, skills and attitudes to manage emotions, set goals, show empathy, build relationships and make responsible decisions. The test of any claim about it is whether you can see the behaviour. 'Waits for a turn to speak in a group of six' passes. 'Has good values' fails.

Four objections come up again and again: no time, it is the counsellor's job, children need discipline, and it is a Western import. Each has a short reply in this section. The deepest shift is from traits to skills. A trait describes a child and stops, while a **skill description contains its own next step**.

left.title: Trait view
items: Writes off children who arrive with less

right.title: Skills view
items: Contains the next step to teach

diagram.caption: the same child, described two ways

key_terms.meaning: Acquiring and applying skills to manage emotions, set goals, show empathy, build relationships and decide well.
US-based organisation, founded 1994, behind the most widely used five-competency framework.
Treats emotional skill as fixed in the child, which lets the school off the hook.
Treats self-control, empathy and cooperation as practised capacities that grow with instruction.
Gandhi's 1937 idea of educating head, heart and hand together through productive work.

worked_example.title: Rewrite a label as a skill
worked_example.setup: A colleague says of a Class 3 child: 'She is shy.' Turn that into a skill description that tells you what to do on Monday.
steps: Ask what the child cannot yet do. She has not yet practised entering a group that is already talking.
Drop the word that describes her and keep the word that describes the skill.
Write the skill version: 'She has not yet practised entering a group that is already talking.'
Now the next step is visible: practise a way into a group, with her, in a small setting.
worked_example.answer: The label 'shy' becomes a named skill gap, and the Monday action follows from the wording.

mistakes: Using labels such as 'aggressive' or 'careless' as if they describe a fixed child. The label ends the conversation, and a skills description starts it.
Defining outcomes you cannot see, such as 'has good values'. If it cannot be observed in behaviour, it cannot be taught deliberately or checked fairly.
Answering 'this is a Western import' with silence. Nai Talim and Shantiniketan made the same argument decades before CASEL existed.
Treating SEL as therapy. It is everyday teaching for all children, while counselling is targeted support for some.

recall.q: What does CASEL stand for?
recall.a: The Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning, a US-based organisation founded in 1994.

recall.q: What test can you apply to any claim about SEL?
recall.a: Can it be observed in a child's behaviour? If the outcome cannot be seen, it cannot be taught deliberately or checked fairly.

recall.q: Why does the skills view matter for equity?
recall.a: A trait view writes off children who arrive with less, while a skills view obliges the school to teach.

recall.q: Name two older traditions the deck links to SEL.
recall.a: Gandhi's Nai Talim (1937) and Tagore's Shantiniketan (1901). Buddhist and Sufi practice also appear.

recall.q: How should you reply to 'we have no time'?
recall.a: The evidence is that SEL does not compete with academics, and the time is largely recovered in fewer disruptions.

sections.title: The Evidence Base for SEL
sections.big_idea: The best evidence is a **2011 meta-analysis**, and the way to use it is to quote its figures exactly and to ask five questions of every claim.
in_plain_words: Durlak and colleagues pooled 213 school-based programmes covering more than 270,000 students. A pooled analysis averages out the luck, small samples and developer bias of any single trial. Its headline is an 11-percentile-point gain in academic achievement against control groups, alongside better skills, attitudes and behaviour and less distress.

Use the number carefully. Eleven percentile points moves a child from the 50th to about the 61st, and it does not mean marks rose by 11 per cent. **186 of the 213 studies were run in the United States**, so the size of the effect in an Indian government school is open. Ask who was studied, whether it was universal, who delivered it and who evaluated it.

diagram.note: a percentile gain is a shift in rank, and a percentage rise in marks is a different claim

key_terms.meaning: A study that pools the results of many separate studies instead of running one new trial.
A step in rank among peers. It differs from a percentage change in marks.
Delivered to whole classes, with no selection of children for difficulty.
Comparison children who did not receive the programme in the same study.
The normal shrinking of effects after a programme stops, which is expected and not a failure.

worked_example.title: Read the figure, check the sample
worked_example.setup: A proposal says SEL gives 11% better marks. Test it against the deck. The figures here are the deck's own.
steps: The study reports an 11-percentile-point gain in achievement, so the proposal has changed the unit.
A child at the 50th percentile moves up: 50 + 11 = 61.
So a middle-ranked child ends near the 61st percentile, which says nothing about marks rising 11 per cent.
Check the sample: 186 of 213 studies were from the United States, and 186 ÷ 213 = 87%.
worked_example.answer: The claim should read 'about 11 percentile points', attributed to Durlak et al. (2011), with the 87% US sample noted.

mistakes: Quoting '11% improvement in academic results'. The figure is percentile points, and the percentage claim is unsupported.
Quoting a return-on-investment ratio built on US incarceration or health costs. Such ratios transfer badly to a district in Bihar.
Expecting one number to apply in every context. It is an average across programmes of varying quality.
Reading fading after the programme as failure. Almost every educational effect shrinks, and the question is whether anything remains.

recall.q: How many programmes and students did Durlak et al. (2011) pool?
recall.a: 213 school-based programmes and more than 270,000 students, from kindergarten to high school.

recall.q: What did the 11-percentile-point gain compare against?
recall.a: Control groups in the same studies.

recall.q: What share of the 213 studies were run in the United States?
recall.a: 186 of them, about 87 per cent.

recall.q: Which outcome would you promise a head teacher first?
recall.a: Conduct and climate, because they move first and everyone in the building can see them.

recall.q: Why is a single year of SEL a weak design?
recall.a: Effects fade, so a thin thread from Class 1 to Class 8 beats one year in Class 3 that is never revisited.

sections.title: The CASEL Framework
sections.big_idea: Five competencies sit inside **four widening rings**, and a school can teach the five faithfully and still undo them through its corridors.
in_plain_words: The five competencies each answer a question. Self-awareness asks what I am feeling. Self-management asks what I do with it. Social awareness asks what is going on for the other person, relationship skills asks how I act on that, and responsible decision-making asks which choice is right for everyone involved. Each supplies something the next needs, so when a child stalls you work backwards to find the missing step.

The five also split into an inside half and a between-people half, with decision-making at the centre. Around them sit four rings: classroom, school, families, community. The wheel is a warning as much as a model. **Work outward from the ring you control**, because waiting for community alignment is a way of never starting.

diagram.caption: four rings around the five competencies, outermost first

key_terms.meaning: The inside half: self-awareness and self-management.
The between-people half: social awareness and relationship skills.
CASEL's picture of five competencies surrounded by four widening settings.
Closest to the child: routines, greetings, how you answer a wrong answer.
A school teaching empathy while running a harsh punitive discipline system.

worked_example.title: Place one incident in the framework
worked_example.setup: Two children fight at break. Use the framework to decide where each child's skill gap lies.
steps: Child A could not settle the anger. That is the inside half, self-management.
Child B misread a joke as contempt. That is the between-people half, social awareness.
The behaviour is identical, but the missing step differs, so the same consequence will fail one of them.
Start with the inside half for the whole class, because a class that can settle itself makes group work possible.
worked_example.answer: Same fight, different missing competency: A needs self-management, B needs social awareness.

mistakes: Waiting for all four rings to line up before starting in your own classroom.
Teaching empathy in a lesson while the school canes both children regardless of what happened. Children follow what the school does.
Repeating the visible behaviour of a stalled child instead of working back down the list to the missing step.
Reading the radar picture as data about a child. The equal values are a memory aid only.

recall.q: Name the five CASEL competencies.
recall.a: Self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship skills and responsible decision-making.

recall.q: What are the four rings of the wheel?
recall.a: Classrooms, schools, families and caregivers, and communities.

recall.q: Which two competencies make up the intrapersonal half?
recall.a: Self-awareness and self-management.

recall.q: Where should a school leader start?
recall.a: With the discipline policy, before the curriculum, since it is cheaper and faster and the curriculum will not take until it changes.

recall.q: Name two free things a teacher can do in the classroom ring.
recall.a: Greet every child by name, keep a predictable lesson order, respond to wrong answers with curiosity, name your own state, or repair after losing your temper.

sections.title: Self-Awareness
sections.big_idea: A child can only steer a feeling once they can **notice it and name it**, and the target is an accurate picture of themselves.
in_plain_words: Self-awareness has four parts: identifying emotions, accurate self-perception, recognising strengths and a sense of purpose. The key word is accurate. A child who believes he is good at everything is as poorly served as one who believes he is good at nothing. Precision in naming matters too, because 'insulted' and 'frustrated' point to different responses where 'angry' points to one reflex.

Practice uses a daily check-in, feelings words in the home language, specific strength-spotting and process praise. Two cautions apply. Never make disclosure compulsory, so 'pass' must be a real option. And never treat a feeling as bad: **every feeling is acceptable and not every action is**. Teachers need this competency as much as children do.

children.label: Identifying emotions
items: Nervous is not the same as angry

children.label: Recognising strengths
items: Specific, tied to what was done
Aim at children with mostly corrections

children.label: Sense of purpose
items: Why an effort is worth making

key_terms.meaning: The words a child has to tell one feeling from another.
Putting words to a feeling gives a moment of choice before reacting.
The belief that ability grows with effort and good strategies (Dweck).
Praise for a specific act or strategy, such as checking your working.
A short daily round on how children feel, where 'pass' is always allowed.

worked_example.title: Turn trait praise into process praise
worked_example.setup: A teacher says 'Brilliant! You are so bright' to a child who finished a test early. Rewrite it so the child learns what to repeat.
steps: Identify what the trait praise says: my worth rides on the next mark.
Find the actual process. The child checked the working before handing it in.
Say it directly: 'You checked your working before handing it in.'
Check there really was a process. Effort praise for easy work backfires.
worked_example.answer: 'You checked your working before handing it in.' names an act the child can repeat.

mistakes: Saying 'Don't be sad, it is nothing.' The child learns the feeling was wrong and hides it next time.
Letting the daily check-in become a roll call. By week three, children give the answer that ends it fastest.
Praising effort on work that was easy. Children read that as consolation and conclude you expect little.
Using 'yet' with no change to the lesson. The word becomes a way of declining to help.

recall.q: Why is self-awareness the first competency?
recall.a: You cannot manage, express or regulate a feeling you cannot first notice and name.

recall.q: What does 'accurate' mean in self-awareness?
recall.a: A self-picture that matches reality closely enough to act on, with neither boast nor collapse.

recall.q: Why do precise words help?
recall.a: 'Angry' suggests one response, while 'insulted' and 'frustrated' suggest different ones, so a child who tells them apart has a real choice.

recall.q: What is the sentence worth practising until automatic?
recall.a: 'You are allowed to be furious with him. You are not allowed to hit him.'

recall.q: What does the deck say about the strength of growth-mindset research?
recall.a: Effects in large replications are real but modest, and largest for students who were struggling.

sections.title: Self-Management
sections.big_idea: Self-management builds control **inside the child**, and it works best when calming tools are taught while everything is calm.
in_plain_words: Self-management means choosing what to do with a feeling: regulating emotion, managing stress, controlling impulses, setting goals and organising to act. Rules put the control outside the child and have to be enforced. This competency builds it inside, where it works in the corridor. Regulation does not stop the spike of emotion. It **shortens the recovery**.

Tools such as slow breathing, a named pause, a calm-down corner and movement all fail when introduced mid-crisis, so rehearse them calm and give each child two options. Stress needs sorting into positive, tolerable and toxic. Breathing exercises suit the first two, and a child facing toxic stress needs protection and material change first. Expect less from younger children and treat the adolescent dip as development.

diagram.caption: goal-setting: the review step is the one that gets dropped

key_terms.meaning: Returning to calm faster after a spike. The spike itself still happens.
Sustained violence, hunger or neglect with no reliable adult.
A safe space any child may use. It works only if it is not a punishment.
The pause between an urge and an action, which grows with practice and maturation.
A predictable schedule and signal that reduce the need to self-regulate from scratch.

worked_example.title: Make a vague hope a goal a Tuesday can hold
worked_example.setup: A child says 'I want to do better in maths.' Use the four boxes to turn it into something to act on.
steps: Want: 'I want to do better in maths.'
Specific goal: 'Practise tables 15 minutes daily.'
Plan: after tea, Monday to Thursday, with my sister checking.
Review on Friday: five minutes on what worked and what to adjust.
worked_example.answer: A goal has an action, a time and place, and someone who will notice, plus a Friday review.

mistakes: Introducing breathing or a pause for the first time in the middle of a meltdown.
Offering a poster of ten strategies. A menu is a task, so two rehearsed options per child work better.
Sending only 'difficult' children to the calm-down corner, which turns it into punishment.
Asking a child to show grit through obstacles the school could remove, such as no light to study by.

recall.q: What does regulation change about an emotional spike?
recall.a: It does not stop the spike. It shortens the recovery and helps the child return to calm faster.

recall.q: Name the three types of stress and what helps each.
recall.a: Positive stress is normal and needs nothing removed. Tolerable stress is buffered by a steady adult. Toxic stress needs protection and material change first.

recall.q: What do the four goal boxes spell out?
recall.a: Want, specific goal, plan and review.

recall.q: Why should adolescents be corrected in private?
recall.a: Peer presence and status raise the stakes, and public correction is met as a challenge to status.

recall.q: Why is structure called kindness?
recall.a: It removes the need to self-regulate from scratch every hour.

sections.title: Social Awareness
sections.big_idea: Social awareness is the ability to read other people, and it matters most when it turns into **action**.
in_plain_words: Social awareness covers perspective-taking, empathy, appreciating diversity, understanding norms and knowing where to find help. The last is the one schools forget, and asking your class who they would go to can be sobering. Perspective-taking is effortful, so it collapses first when a child is angry. Ask for it ten minutes after a fight, never during one.

Empathy understands what another feels, and it differs from pity, which preserves the gap it appears to close. Charity framing in a mixed classroom teaches pity and rank. In an Indian classroom, caste, religion, language, disability and gender all show up in ordinary weeks, so **name difference with respect**. Most children who do nothing lack a script, a partner or confidence that the adult will back them.

right.title: Pity
items: Preserves the gap it appears to close

diagram.caption: compassion is empathy that moves to action

key_terms.meaning: Imagining how a situation looks and feels to someone whose experience differs from yours.
Sensing and understanding what another feels, without needing to agree.
Empathy that moves to action, which is what SEL aims at.
Being included. Who eats alone is a reliable sign of exclusion.
Mixing under fair, cooperative conditions, which reduces prejudice.

worked_example.title: Check a group task for the four conditions
worked_example.setup: A teacher sets a mixed-group project: one child leads, four listen, and the best group wins a prize. Test it against the four conditions for contact to reduce prejudice.
steps: Equal standing: one leader and four listeners fails it. Give every child a real role.
Shared goal: the group succeeds together, which the project does provide.
Cooperation without competition: a prize for beating other groups fails it. Remove the prize.
Adult sanction: the teacher should visibly back the mixing and rotate roles.
worked_example.answer: The task meets one condition of four, so redesign it with real roles, no prize and visible adult backing.

mistakes: Asking a bullied or harassed child to see the harasser's point of view as the first move. Safety and acknowledgement come first.
Letting children pick teams in public, which teaches the last-chosen child something about themselves every time.
Teaching empathy through charity lessons in which the 'less fortunate' are sitting in the room.
Staying silent about caste. Silence removes the teacher from the conversation the children are already having.

recall.q: Name the five parts of social awareness.
recall.a: Perspective-taking, empathy, appreciating diversity, understanding norms and identifying supports.

recall.q: What is the most useful question in a playground dispute?
recall.a: 'What did each of you want? Not who was right.'

recall.q: Give two of the four conditions for contact to reduce prejudice.
recall.a: Equal standing in the task, a shared goal, cooperation not competition, adult sanction.

recall.q: Which two sentences does the deck suggest rehearsing?
recall.a: 'Come and sit with us' and 'That is not funny.'

recall.q: What is the most reliable single sign of exclusion?
recall.a: A child who eats alone.

sections.title: Relationship Skills
sections.big_idea: Relationship skills turn awareness into action, and their core is **structured conflict resolution** that both children get to be heard in.
in_plain_words: The six parts are communicating clearly, listening actively, cooperating, resisting social pressure, resolving conflict and seeking or offering help. Teach 'I' statements as a feeling plus a specific event. Cooperation depends on task design: a task one person could do alone will be done by one person. Conflict is normal, and the usual school responses of punishing both or forcing an apology teach children to hide it.

The four-step sequence is cool down, each speaks, each listens, solve together. The listening step does the work. It takes twelve minutes the first time and two by the tenth. Peer mediation suits disputes between equals only. Where one child has power over another, as in bullying, the work is for adults, and **the watching bystanders are where the behaviour is licensed or refused**.

diagram.caption: the conflict sequence that draws on every earlier competency

key_terms.meaning: A feeling plus the specific event, in place of an accusation.
Attending fully, then reflecting the other's point back before answering.
Trained students helping classmates settle small disputes between equals.
A child who watches. The majority role in bullying and the main source of influence.
A break in a relationship and the explicit step of mending it.

worked_example.title: Rewrite an accusation as an 'I' statement
worked_example.setup: A child says 'You always leave me out.' Rewrite it as a feeling plus a specific event, and check both halves are present.
steps: Find the feeling: left out.
Find the specific event: you three went ahead at break.
Join them: 'I felt left out when you three went ahead at break.'
Check both halves. 'I feel that you are an idiot' fails the test.
worked_example.answer: 'I felt left out when you three went ahead at break.' keeps the talk on the problem.

mistakes: Treating 'say no' as enough for peer pressure. It costs the child their place in the group.
Running bully-victim mediation. It repeats the harm with the school's authority behind it.
Handing bullying or anything with a power gap to a twelve-year-old mediator.
Skipping the listening step because the bell is coming. It is the step that does the work.

recall.q: List the four steps of the conflict sequence.
recall.a: Cool down, each speaks, each listens, solve together.

recall.q: Why do 'I' statements work?
recall.a: Nobody can deny your account of your own experience, so the conversation stays on the problem.

recall.q: What is cooperation a property of?
recall.a: The task. Put cooperative children on a solo task and one will do it alone.

recall.q: Who has the most influence in a bullying situation?
recall.a: The bystanders, the majority of the class, whose silence sustains it and whose response ends it.

recall.q: Who gains most from peer mediation training?
recall.a: The mediators, who improve more than those mediated.

sections.title: Responsible Decision-Making
sections.big_idea: This competency is where the other four are spent, and the aim is **reasons that hold when no one is watching**.
in_plain_words: Responsible decision-making weighs ethical standards, safety, consequences, the wellbeing of others and a realistic evaluation of what happened last time. Compliance produces good behaviour while observed. Reasoning produces judgement in situations nobody wrote a rule for. A child trained only to obey is equally available to be led anywhere, so reasons need to be attached to rules and questioned.

Teach it with a four-step loop: stop, list options, think through consequences for everyone affected, then choose and reflect. Children usually miss the other person tomorrow and the cost to someone not in the room. Use real, anonymised dilemmas from last week and announce no answer. The same habits scale from playground to citizenship, and **a programme that measures success by how little children push back has inverted the aim**.

diagram.caption: reflection feeds the next decision point

key_terms.meaning: Behaviour that follows rules while observed.
Judging a new situation by fairness, harm and care.
What happens next for me and for others, widened in time and in who counts.
A realistic case with no single announced answer, used to build judgement.
The same decision skill at larger scales, up to citizenship.

worked_example.title: Run the four steps on a real class problem
worked_example.setup: Children hurry to leave the room and shared equipment is never returned. Use the problem-solving frame the deck gives.
steps: Define the problem without blame: 'the equipment is missing at the end of lesson.' A culprit's name means it is not yet a problem statement.
Generate options with no judging, including silly ones.
Weigh consequences by asking who each option affects as well as whether it works.
Choose and act: someone specific does something specific by a specific time. Then review.
worked_example.answer: A defined problem, options, weighed consequences and a named owner, with a return visit so it is not theatre.

mistakes: Judging the first suggestion. The class stops offering, and the session becomes a guess about what the teacher wants.
Announcing the correct view at the end of a dilemma. Children then start guessing at the right answer and stop reasoning.
Using distant dilemmas about strangers, which are comfortable and produce little reasoning.
Reducing the competency to rule-following because rules are easier to observe.

recall.q: What five things does responsible decision-making weigh?
recall.a: Ethical standards, safety, consequences, the wellbeing of others and realistic evaluation.

recall.q: What is the uncomfortable last row of compliance versus reasoning?
recall.a: Obedience transfers to any authority, while judgement can also refuse an authority.

recall.q: Give two consequences a child usually misses.
recall.a: How the other person will feel tomorrow, the effect on a friendship over a term, the cost to someone not in the room, what happens if everyone does it.

recall.q: Who speaks last in a dilemma discussion?
recall.a: The teacher, who gives an opinion last if at all.

recall.q: What does the incident table show about the five competencies?
recall.a: One incident uses all five, so a failure at the last step often traces back to an earlier missing one.

sections.title: Implementing SEL
sections.big_idea: Programmes work when they are **Sequenced, Active, Focused and Explicit**, and most failures are visible before they start.
in_plain_words: SAFE comes from Durlak et al. (2011): connected step-by-step activities, active forms of learning, time set aside for skill development and explicit targeting of named skills. Posters and one-off assemblies fail all four. Add a fifth question: who delivers it and what training do they get? Strong programmes combine explicit lessons with integration, because integration alone is easy to claim without doing.

A whole-school approach means shared language, aligned discipline, leadership that can explain SEL, adults modelling the skills and non-teaching staff included. Quality of delivery, meaning fidelity and enough time, often matters more than which programme you pick. Teachers need their own support, because **an exhausted adult models dysregulation several times a day**. Start small: a daily check-in, then one row at a time.

diagram.caption: four features Durlak et al. found in programmes that worked

key_terms.meaning: Sequenced, Active, Focused, Explicit: four features of programmes that work.
Dedicated lessons that directly teach a skill.
SEL woven into ordinary teaching, such as cooperative maths.
Following the programme's design as intended.
Enough time with the programme.

worked_example.title: Apply SAFE to three offers
worked_example.setup: A vendor offers an annual motivational assembly, posters in every corridor and a ten-week sequenced curriculum with role-play.
steps: Annual assembly: fails all four features, so expect nothing.
Posters: not active and not focused, so they are decoration.
Ten-week sequenced curriculum with role-play: passes, so ask about teacher training next.
Add the fifth question for the winner: who delivers it and with what training?
worked_example.answer: Only the ten-week curriculum passes, and it still needs a check on teacher training.

mistakes: Calling SEL 'fully integrated' without being able to say which skill was taught last week.
Buying a packaged curriculum and skipping teacher training. The training budget under five per cent of the total is a warning sign.
Contradicting SEL with harsh punitive discipline.
Trying all four 'this week, month, term, year' rows in September and abandoning all by November.

recall.q: What does SAFE stand for?
recall.a: Sequenced, Active, Focused and Explicit.

recall.q: Why does integration alone often fail?
recall.a: It needs no timetable change, so it can be claimed without doing anything and skills go unnamed and untaught.

recall.q: What is the cheapest useful support for teachers?
recall.a: Fifteen minutes a fortnight to discuss a difficult child without being assessed on it.

recall.q: What does the 'this week' row of the start-small table list?
recall.a: A daily check-in, greeting by name and one predictable routine, at five minutes a day.

recall.q: Which pitfall's warning sign is 'it is in the annual calendar and missing from the weekly timetable'?
recall.a: Treating SEL as a one-off event.

sections.title: Measuring SEL: with Care
sections.big_idea: Measure to improve and never to rank, because attaching **stakes to SEL scores** corrupts the measure and can teach children not to disclose.
in_plain_words: Decide the purpose before the instrument, and write down what the data may not be used for. Legitimate uses include understanding a class, checking a programme and noticing a child who needs support. Illegitimate uses include ranking children, appraising teachers, screening admissions and reporting a district target. Each method has an unfit use: self-report cannot judge an individual child, and teacher report cannot compare across teachers.

Self-report has special limits. Children answer as they think they should, and a child who grows more self-aware may rate herself lower, so progress can read as decline. Goodhart's law explains why high stakes corrupt: **when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure**. Check items for cultural bias, protect privacy, report at class or school level, and if you cannot meet all five principles, measure climate and delivery only.

children.label: Teacher report
items: Good for change in one class

key_terms.meaning: Answering as you think you should, which drifts scores toward what is wanted.
A measure that becomes a target stops being a good measure.
Use several methods and treat disagreement between them as information.
Attaching a score to rankings, appraisal or funding.
A one-page document with purposes, prohibited uses and privacy rules.

worked_example.title: Classify five uses of an SEL score
worked_example.setup: A district proposes five uses of a class-level SEL survey. Sort each into legitimate or illegitimate.
steps: Helping a teacher understand a class: legitimate.
Ranking schools against each other: illegitimate, and schools will coach the answers.
Checking whether a programme is working: legitimate.
Paying teachers by score: illegitimate, and teachers rate their own classes generously.
Noticing a child who needs support: legitimate, with the data kept inside the school.
worked_example.answer: Three of the five are legitimate. Ranking and pay turn the survey into a target and corrupt it.

mistakes: Building a tool for the left column of the purposes table and letting someone use it for the right a year later.
Reading a fall in self-report scores as programme failure. What fell may be children's willingness to overrate themselves.
Scoring 'makes eye contact' as a skill, when lowering the eyes to an elder is respect in many families.
Putting an SEL score on a child's record, which teaches children not to disclose feeling unsafe.

recall.q: Why decide the purpose before the instrument?
recall.a: Almost every harm follows from a tool built for one purpose being used for another, usually later and by someone who was not in the original conversation.

recall.q: Why can a self-report score fall when a child has improved?
recall.a: A child who becomes more self-aware sees more to improve and rates herself lower.

recall.q: What does the deck advise if you cannot meet all five principles?
recall.a: Measure climate and programme delivery only, and leave individual skills unmeasured.

recall.q: How should data be protected from gaming?
recall.a: Keep it inside the school, aggregated across the class, and unconnected to anyone's money or promotion.

recall.q: What check should you run on any instrument?
recall.a: Read every item aloud with two teachers from the community you serve and ask which ones would score their own childhood as deficient.

sections.title: SEL in South Asia & India
sections.big_idea: Adapt, do not copy: keep the **skill being practised** and rebuild the situation, language and examples around the children in front of you.
in_plain_words: NEP 2020 names socio-emotional learning and the all-round development of learners, which gives you policy language to use with a sceptical head teacher. Its progress cards are also the most likely route by which SEL becomes graded and ranked. The deck names no programme as a success, because such claims go stale, so check any scheme locally through your state SCERT and DIET.

Imported curricula carry assumptions about homes, space, names and sleepovers. Translation alone does not fix them, since a translated sleepover scenario is still a sleepover scenario. Framings differ too: individualist and interdependent views each carry a risk, so hold on to three things that survive both. In an unequal setting, ask whether **a skill is missing or the environment makes it impossible**, read behaviour through a trauma-informed lens, and teach feelings in the mother tongue.

diagram.caption: from national policy to what the child meets

key_terms.meaning: India's policy, which emphasises socio-emotional learning and the all-round development of learners.
Rebuilding stories, names and dilemmas around local children, with the skill kept.
Asking what the child has been through in place of what is wrong with them.
Centres family, community, duty and respect in place of the individual.
A NEP 2020 item including self-assessment that could become one more ranking.

worked_example.title: Adapt one imported scenario
worked_example.setup: An imported lesson says 'Talk to your parents about your feelings' and uses a sleepover scenario. Adapt both using the deck's table.
steps: Spot the assumption in the first line: a two-adult home with time and privacy.
Widen it to any trusted adult, including elders and siblings.
Spot the assumption in the sleepover: a social form most children will not recognise.
Rewrite the situation around a wedding, a festival or a shared courtyard, and keep the same skill.
worked_example.answer: The skill stays and the situation is rebuilt, ideally by teachers in an afternoon, so they own it.

mistakes: Treating a translated scenario as adapted. The assumptions travel with the words.
Citing a state programme without checking it still runs, what its reach is and who evaluated it.
Teaching 'self-control' to hungry children. Fix the midday meal first.
Reading a child's silence or flat reaction as misconduct when it may be a stress response.

recall.q: What does NEP 2020 open for SEL, and what does it leave open?
recall.a: It names SEL as policy and gives curricular space for life skills. It leaves open who trains teachers and how the space survives board-exam pressure.

recall.q: Why does the deck name no programme as a success?
recall.a: Claims in this space go stale within a year or two, and repeating them misinforms people who trusted the resource.

recall.q: What three things survive translation between the individualist and interdependent framings?
recall.a: Every child can name what they feel, say no to harm, and answer for the effect they have on others.

recall.q: What question should you ask before any intervention aimed at one child?
recall.a: Is this skill missing, or is this environment making the skill impossible?

recall.q: Where does a teacher refer suspected abuse or self-harm?
recall.a: To the school's child-protection route and to trained help, today.

notes.2: Use this agenda as a **map for choosing where to start**. Sections 4 to 8 are the reference half, one competency each. Sections 9 to 11 are the decision half. If a programme, budget or assessment is on your desk this week, jump to those three sections first.
notes.4: Read the definition clause by clause, because each one does work. The eight-year-old column turns an abstract list into things you could see on Monday. Keep the test in mind: **if you cannot observe it in behaviour, you cannot teach it deliberately** or judge it fairly.
notes.5: A framework is a vocabulary, so pick one and use it consistently. The four rows show these frameworks describe the same human capacities from different starting points. The one place the choice bites is measurement: **choose the framework first, then the assessment**, never the reverse.
notes.6: Follow the four boxes as a chain: safe, attending, engaged, learning. The table shows how a worried child spends attention on threat before the lesson gets any. The classroom conclusion is that **regulation comes first**. Keep your claims at 'emotion and attention interact' and the argument holds.
notes.7: Learn the four objections together with their replies, because you will hear them at staff meetings. The reply to 'no time' is that disruptions drop, and the reply to 'Western import' is Nai Talim. Note the serious objection at the bottom: **SEL must not stop at the child**.
notes.8: This slide trains one habit: rewrite a label as a skill. 'Aggressive' ends the conversation, while 'few strategies for anger' tells you what to teach. Try it today on the **three labels you use most**. The equity point is that only the skills view obliges the school to act.
notes.9: Use this slide when someone calls SEL foreign. Three older traditions made related claims, and each row says what the claim was. Be exact about what is new: evidence, teachable parts, and the finding on how a programme is run. Say 'commonly attributed' for the quotation, as the slide does.
notes.10: Read the last table first, since it says what you will be able to do after each part. Then choose your route by time. With one hour, take **Section 3 for the framework, Section 9 for the SAFE test and Section 11 for the cautions**. Those three change practice most.
notes.12: Remember three numbers: 213 programmes, over 270,000 students, published 2011. A meta-analysis pools many studies, which averages out luck and developer bias. Then hold the limitation: **186 of the 213 were run in the United States**, so the size of the effect in an Indian government school remains open.
notes.13: The figure is 11 percentile points, so a child at the 50th percentile moves to about the 61st. That differs from 11 per cent more marks. Always attach the source. The finding that matters to a head teacher is that **SEL time did not come out of academics**.
notes.14: Read the chart as direction only, since the slide says the magnitudes are illustrative. The point to carry away is that several outcomes rise together. If a proposal quotes bar heights as effect sizes, **treat that as a misreading** and send the writer back to the paper.
notes.15: Six outcome areas appear in the table, from skills and attitudes to conduct, distress and marks. The explanation for moving so many is that SEL sits upstream of all of them. For a first conversation with a sceptic, **promise conduct and climate**, because those move first and everyone sees them.
notes.16: Follow the table down the rows: gains at the end, smaller gains a year on, and persisting gains years later. Fading after an intervention is normal, so ask what remains. The planning lesson is to **spread SEL thinly across many years**, which beats one intense year that is never revisited.
notes.17: The economic case points in a favourable direction, though no single ratio deserves trust. The table ranks the sources of savings by how solid they are, from discipline incidents (direct) to long-run justice costs (modelled). Your defensible move is **your own school's before-and-after count**.
notes.18: Two columns of claims, then a four-question appraisal you can use on any brochure. Ask who was studied, whether it was universal or targeted, who delivered it and who evaluated it. A vendor who cannot answer **has already told you something**. The fifth question concerns the comparison group.
notes.19: SEL has spread widely, and the slide separates the frame from the furniture. The framework, the SAFE test and the whole-school argument travel. Scripts, names and assumptions about class size do not. Check any imported programme by asking **which part is frame and which part is furniture**.
notes.21: Memorise the five as five questions: what am I feeling, what do I do with it, what is going on for them, how do I act on that, and which choice is right. The order carries meaning. When a child stalls, **work backwards down the list** to find the missing step.
notes.22: The radar is a memory aid and carries no data. Its equal values only show that the five support each other. Do not read it as a profile of a real child. Redraw it for your own class only if you have actual observations to put on it.
notes.23: Sort the five into two halves: inside (awareness, management) and between people (social awareness, relationships), with decision-making at the centre. Use the halves for diagnosis, since the same fight can come from either side. For a whole class, **start with the inside half**.
notes.24: The wheel puts the five competencies inside four rings: classroom, school, family, community. The table names the lever you control in each. The practical rule is in the last line: **start with the ring you control** and work outward, because waiting for all four means never starting.
notes.25: Everything in the table is free and can start Monday. Greeting by name, a predictable lesson, curiosity about wrong answers, naming your own state and repairing after you lose your temper each teach a skill without a lesson. They are also hard to do in a class of sixty, which Section 9 addresses.
notes.26: Read each row as a pair: what the lesson says and what the school does. Children believe the school's behaviour. If you lead a school, **change the discipline policy before you buy a curriculum**, because until it changes the lessons will not take root.
notes.27: The left column shows common practice and the right shows a swap you can make this term. The best swap costs minutes: one specific piece of good news per child per term. Notice the pattern that **partnership works through what the school already sends home**, since it needs no attendance.
notes.28: The outer ring extends practice in time, because a school holds a child for only part of the day and none of the holidays. Use the table to list who in your area could reinforce the same skills. Keep the caution: **alignment means shared language**, and outsourcing the work to a visiting session fails.
notes.30: Self-awareness comes first because a feeling must be noticed and named before it can be steered. The table splits it into four observable parts. Underline the word 'accurate': the target is a **self-picture close enough to reality to act on**, with neither boasting nor collapse.
notes.31: Precision is the mechanism. 'Angry' invites one response, while 'insulted' and 'frustrated' invite different ones, so a child with both words has a choice. Work from the table's left column to the right with your class. Start in the **home language**, where finer distinctions already exist.
notes.32: Four practices, each paired with a trap. The common trap is the check-in that becomes a roll call, as children learn which answer ends it fastest. **Vary the format** with a number, weather word or colour, and keep 'pass' a real option so disclosure is never compulsory.
notes.33: Make strength-spotting specific to what the child did. The table lists strengths a school seldom records and where you would see each one. Aim the practice at children whose records are mostly correction, since **they are the least likely to receive it by chance**.
notes.34: Growth mindset is a lens on difficulty: the table shows a fixed reading and a growth reading of the same event. Keep the slide's honesty about the research, which reports modest effects. Mindset sits beside good teaching and never replaces it, and 'yet' offered with no help is a way of declining to teach.
notes.35: The table reverses what you probably say. Trait praise ties worth to the next mark, while praise for a specific act gives the child something to repeat. Try the one-week experiment: **write down what you said to your three most-praised children**. Praise process only where a process existed.
notes.36: Read the left column as your own early warning signs: rising voice, sarcasm, a punishment you would not defend later, dread of one child's lesson. Choose two that fit you. **Noticing early** is the whole skill, and repairing afterwards teaches more than never slipping.
notes.37: Each well-meant phrase in the table teaches a child to hide the feeling. Hold one sentence ready: **'You are allowed to be furious. You are not allowed to hit him.'** It keeps both halves. Also watch your own class for the gendered pattern the last paragraph describes.
notes.39: Self-management is the choosing step after noticing. The table gives a visible version of each part, from calming in minutes to starting a task unprompted. Note the contrast with rules: rules place control outside the child, while this builds it inside, where it works when you are absent.
notes.40: Read the two curves as a comparison, and keep in mind that the values are illustrative. A regulated child still spikes but returns faster. That sets your goal: **shorten the recovery**, since you cannot remove the spike. Judge progress by how fast a child returns to calm.
notes.41: Each strategy in the table fails the same way when it is introduced in the middle of a crisis. So **teach calming tools when everything is calm**, as a whole-class routine. Give each child two options they chose, because a menu of ten becomes one more task.
notes.42: Sort stress into three kinds using the table. Positive stress needs no removal and tolerable stress needs a steady adult. Toxic stress needs protection and material change first. The decision rule is that breathing exercises suit the first two and **cannot substitute for safety**.
notes.43: Use the age table to set realistic expectations before you correct anyone. A five-year-old needs the pause named aloud, and an adolescent reacts to status in front of peers. For adolescents the practical rule is **correct privately**, because public correction invites a defence of status.
notes.44: Follow the four boxes from want to review. The right-hand column of the table shares three features: a specific action, a time and place, and someone who will notice. Add the review step, **a five-minute Friday check**, or goal-setting becomes a yearly ritual.
notes.45: Persistence mostly means having a next move. The table swaps blame for a question that points at the stuck part. Teach a second strategy and skip the urging. Keep the caution about 'grit': do not ask a child to push through **obstacles the school could remove**.
notes.46: Five routines, each doing regulation on the child's behalf. Choose the visible schedule and the quiet signal first, since they cost nothing and cut incidents. Remember the closing line: structure means predictability. A noisy room with **reliable rules regulates better than a silent one** run on the adult's mood.
notes.48: Social awareness turns the lens outward, with five parts listed in the table. Spend time on the last row, identifying supports: it carries immediate safeguarding value. Try asking your class **who they would go to** for help. Treat apparent rudeness as possibly a child reading an unfamiliar rulebook.
notes.49: Four terms, ordered by how they relate to action: empathy understands, sympathy feels from outside, pity adds distance, compassion moves to action. The aim of SEL is the last. Remember that **empathy is not agreement**, which matters most when you teach adolescents.
notes.50: Four prompts to use in ordinary lessons, with when each fits. The best one is 'what did each of you want?', which replaces 'who was right?'. Perspective-taking is effortful, so ask for it **ten minutes after a fight**, and never first from a child who was harassed.
notes.51: Use the table as an observation list. Each row names something you can watch for in an ordinary week, so pick one and watch it for five days. The slide's principle is to **name difference with respect**, since silence about caste leaves children to have that conversation without you.
notes.52: Four questions you can answer by watching, with no survey. Who eats alone is the most reliable sign of exclusion. Who is chosen last tells you about your grouping method. The fix at the bottom is simple: **assign groups yourself** so no child is picked last in public.
notes.53: The four conditions are equal standing, a shared goal, cooperation and adult backing. Contact without them can harden prejudice, since a mixed group where one child works confirms the old belief. Check your next group task against the list and **rotate the roles**.
notes.54: Most children notice distress, and the table shows four reasons they still do nothing. Match the fix to the block: a script, a partner, a named responsibility or a visible adult response. Teach two lines and rehearse them: **'Come and sit with us' and 'That is not funny.'**
notes.56: Relationship skills are where awareness becomes action. The table lists six observable parts. Linger on resisting pressure, which costs a child their place in the group, so 'just say no' is an expensive instruction. Asking for help is also a skill that **mocked children stop using**.
notes.57: The table converts accusations into statements about your own experience. Teach the form as a feeling plus a specific event, and check both halves are present. The reason is practical: **nobody can deny your account of your feelings**, so the talk stays on the problem.
notes.58: Cooperation depends on task design. Each failing pattern in the table has a design fix, such as named roles, a speaking role for the quiet child, or a task needing more than one person. If group work seems not to work, **fix the task first**. Class jobs give practice with no lesson time.
notes.59: Compare what each school response teaches. Punishing both, believing the louder child and forcing a handshake all teach the child to hide conflict. The last row teaches that adults are worth going to. Ask 'what would make this right?' in place of demanding an apology, and **watch for power gaps**.
notes.60: Learn the four steps: cool down, each speaks, each listens, solve together. The listening step does the work and is the one people skip. Expect twelve minutes the first time and two by the tenth. The sequence is proof that **the five competencies work as one system**.
notes.61: Peer mediation succeeds under four conditions: training, small disputes, adult debriefing and a rotating role. The line to hold sits in the third paragraph: **children mediate disputes between equals**. Power imbalance, repetition or possible harm belong to adults, whatever a brochure says.
notes.62: Read the table as a map of influence: the bystanders are most of the class. Punishment reaches the smallest group, while a class that responds with 'stop' ends the behaviour. Remember the firm rule at the bottom: **never run bully-victim mediation**.
notes.63: The teacher-student bond is the most powerful lever in the school, and the table lists four near-free ways to build it. Do the second row this fortnight and notice the child you have not spoken to. This bond also **outlasts the funded programme**, the curriculum and the trainer.
notes.65: Responsible decision-making weighs five things, each written in a child's words. Use those questions with students directly. Note the warning that schools reduce this competency to rule-following because it is easier to see. The difference shows when **no one is watching**.
notes.66: Compare the two columns: compliance gives good behaviour while observed, while reasoning gives judgement in new situations. The last row is the uncomfortable one, since a child trained only to obey can be led anywhere. Keep rules for safety and young children, and **attach reasons that can be questioned**.
notes.67: Follow the four boxes, then read the table as a list of what children miss: the other person tomorrow, the friendship over a term, the absent party, the effect if everyone did it. Practise with **last week's actual problem**, anonymised, because invented cases are treated as fiction.
notes.68: Five steps with a rule for each. The rule most often broken is the second: no evaluating while options are generated. If you judge the first suggestion, the class stops offering. Use the frame on a real class problem so children see that **the outcome will change something**.
notes.69: Match a dilemma to the age band, then run it by three rules: no answer announced, disagreement welcome, teacher speaks last. Once children expect the correct view at the end, they guess in place of reasoning. Choose dilemmas **close to this class this term**, which are harder to chair and better.
notes.70: The same skill appears at four scales, from playground to citizenship. The slide links SEL to civic education. Hold the last paragraph as a test of your programme: if success is measured by **how little children push back**, the programme has inverted the aim.
notes.71: Read the table as a diagnostic. Each step in one incident uses a different competency, and a failure at the last row often traces back three rows. Ask 'which step could he not do?' before choosing a consequence. This is **the reason the five are taught together**.
notes.73: Compare the two routes by what each needs and how each fails. Explicit lessons name a skill and integration makes it stick. Integration alone is easiest to claim without doing, so ask 'which skill was taught last week?' The workable answer is **one short explicit slot plus one daily place to use it**.
notes.74: SAFE is four questions: is it sequenced, active, focused and explicit? Use the failing column to spot each fault in a brochure. This finding from Durlak et al. converts a vague wish for quality into something you can check in **two minutes**.
notes.75: Run the five common offers in the table through SAFE. An assembly, a poster or a general claim of integration fails, while a ten-week sequence with role-play passes. Then add the fifth question: **who delivers it and how are they trained**? Untrained teachers can sink a good curriculum.
notes.76: The table gives a test of reality for each element, such as whether two teachers use the same words and whether the head can explain SEL unprompted. The last row is the one skipped, and the gate is where children spend unsupervised time. If you are alone, **find one colleague**.
notes.77: The bars are illustrative and show one pattern: the same programme gives very different results depending on how faithfully and how long it is run. So ask about fidelity and dosage before you ask about brand. **Quality of delivery often matters more than which programme you choose**.
notes.78: Teachers are the delivery mechanism, so their stress is a delivery risk. Compare the two columns: what teachers need and what programmes give. The cheapest fix is on the slide: fifteen minutes a fortnight to discuss a hard case **with no assessment attached**.
notes.79: Five pitfalls, each paired with an early warning you can spot before the programme starts. Bring the list to the meeting where the decision is made. If SEL seems not to work, **check the list before blaming the children or the idea**.
notes.80: Pick one row of the timetable and finish it before the next. The first two rows cost nothing and need no permission. They also produce most of the visible change in climate. Avoid the failure at the bottom: **four starts in September, four abandoned by November**.
notes.82: Before you measure, write the purpose. The table pairs each legitimate use with the illegitimate use it tends to slide toward. Put in writing what the data **may not be used for**, because pressure to use numbers for ranking arrives once they exist.
notes.83: Read the third column of each table: every method has a use and an unfit use. No single method is enough, so combine them. When self-report and teacher report disagree, **that gap is information**, often about a relationship, so avoid averaging it away.
notes.84: Five distortions of self-report appear in the table. The costly one is the third: a child who grows more self-aware rates herself lower, so progress can read as decline. State in advance how you will read a fall. Use self-report as a **conversation starter**, never as a verdict.
notes.85: High stakes corrupt the measure, and the table shows what happens within a year to each use. The last row is the most serious: a child learns that honesty about feeling unsafe goes on a record. Keep this one rule: **do not attach an SEL score to anything consequential**.
notes.86: Goodhart's law is the reason for the caution in the previous slide. The three examples show ordinary staff gaming a target with no dishonesty involved. Protect your data structurally: keep it **inside the school, aggregated and unconnected to money or promotion**.
notes.87: For each item in the table, ask what else could explain a low score. Eye contact, assertiveness and stillness differ by family, gender and neurology. Before using any instrument, do the minimum check: read each item with **two teachers from the community** you serve.
notes.88: Five principles, each with what it looks like on paper. Turn them into a one-page measurement plan, which protects children after the person who started the programme leaves. If you cannot meet all five, use the fallback: **measure climate and delivery only**.
notes.90: NEP 2020 gives SEL national backing, and the table splits what it opens from what it leaves open. Quote the policy language to a head teacher who ignores meta-analyses. Watch the fourth row: **progress cards could turn SEL into a ranked, graded thing**.
notes.91: The deck names no programme as a success, deliberately, since such claims go stale. Use the four checks in the table before citing any scheme: is it still running, what is its real reach, who evaluated it, and what did teachers receive? Then **verify locally** through your SCERT, DIET and neighbouring schools.
notes.92: Adaptation is a rebuild around the skill. The table shows imported assumptions: a quiet space, a private two-adult home, a sleepover. Gather teachers for an afternoon, hand them the skill list and let them **write the scenarios**. The material fits better and the teachers own it.
notes.93: The table sets two framings side by side, and the deck calls neither more advanced. Each has a risk: one breeds indifference, the other can silence a child, especially about harm at home. Keep the three things that survive in both: **name feelings, say no to harm, answer for your effect on others**.
notes.94: The left column is what happens when a child-focused framework meets an unequal setting unexamined. The right column starts with conditions. Use the question at the bottom before every intervention aimed at one child: **is this skill missing, or is the environment making it impossible?**
notes.95: Behaviour can be read as misconduct or as a stress response, and the table pairs each with its reading. The middle column tends to make things worse. Limits still hold, since the child still repairs. Know your edge: **suspected abuse or self-harm goes to child protection today**.
notes.96: Emotion lives in the first language, so teach feelings there. The four practices cost almost nothing. Without them, a feelings check-in becomes **a test of English scored as a test of feeling**. You need not teach in every language, only avoid forcing a child to perform in one they are still acquiring.
notes.97: Five constraints, each with a realistic response. The pattern is to choose less and sustain it: two practices beat a full programme abandoned. Build your own evidence, and test any claim of SEL by asking **what changed in the timetable**. If nothing did, nothing changed.
notes.98: Use this as a final checklist and pick one row. All five are doable by one teacher this term without a budget. The closing warning is the same as in Section 10: **never attach an SEL score** to a child's record, a teacher's appraisal or school funding.
notes.99: This is a reading list with a use for each source. If you read one thing, read the 2011 meta-analysis itself, since it is the source of the two most misquoted numbers. The Taylor et al. paper answers whether effects last. Pair this deck with the three ImpactMojo courses named on the slide.
